units.spine: Nothing presses Rundgate at present, and the quiet is not luck. The town is kept ready, and a town kept this ready is not worth the price of trying.

units.poolKey: Invasion & War: walls AND professional garrison
units.spine: A stranger is stopped at the gates and counted before he is let through, and what he is let into is a town with walls it holds and soldiers it pays.
faces: A man on one of the gates says a stranger pays the gate. What the gate owes the hall is settled between the two of them, in the gate's own time.
A woman who keeps the hall books holds that a stranger who has paid at the gate has paid the town, whatever the men at the gate tell him.
A clerk of one of the courts says anyone who paid the toll may argue it in court, a stranger as readily as a carter.
A traveller found his pack opened at the gate and nothing taken out of it but the toll.
An innkeeper says the town has never been asked whether it wants soldiers, only what the soldiers cost it.

units.spine: Rundgate keeps a court and nowhere to hold a man overnight, so what the law here takes from him is his money or his place in the town.
faces: One of the watch says what turns up after dark is dealt with after dark, there being nowhere to leave a man until morning.
A bailiff says the court hears in daylight what the watch settled in the dark, and nobody asks the court first.
A clerk in the hall reckons the purse does not run to a room to hold men in and never has. He does not say who asked for one.
A stallholder says a short weight goes to the court and comes back as a sum to pay, and the scales it was weighed on stay where they are.
A parish warden holds that the parish has a place for a man once he is dead and the town has none for him while he lives.
The guild master says a sum paid out of a man's takings is forgotten, and the mark it leaves on his work is not.
A carter at one of the taverns reckons a man with a house here pays the sum and stays, and a man without one is told to go.
A drover says there is nothing here to take from a man who owns nothing in the town, and the town is left with the one thing it can do with him.
A gatekeeper says the men on the gates are handed a man and a direction and no reason for either.
A serjeant of the garrison holds that what comes at the town is the garrison's business and the men walked out of the gates are not.

units.spine: Anyone in the town has seen the grain store kept stocked, and takes it that a crisis would find the place ready.
faces: One of the aldermen says the hall asks the trades for no more than the trades can carry.
A warden of one of the guilds says the carrying is the trades' and the asking is not.
The guilds' account is the likelier of the two, the hall having a purse to defend and the trades only a bill to pay.
A night patrolman holds that the rounds are kept by men who are owed for keeping them.
Whoever keeps the toll book says a cart bound for the grain store is not kept waiting, whatever else is.
A rider who stopped a night heard the grain store praised and the watch's wage complained of by the same people.
A potboy of the district says the watch is a trade that drinks on what it is owed.
A man who draws the wage holds that a town able to feed itself through a crisis and unable to pay him in full has decided something it has not said.
At the markets the people who deal there say the hall is settled with before anybody settles anything of their own.
A canon holds that the town keeps its word to the dead before it keeps its word to the living.

units.poolKey: Disasters & Famine: granary AND parish care only
units.spine: The town keeps a full grain store and no house for the sick, so whoever tends the sick here comes out of the church.
faces: A priest of one of the parishes holds that a stranger asks for a house for the sick and is given a person instead, and nobody born here asks for the house.
Grain is hard to keep in this town, the stallholders say, for anybody without a door of their own to keep it behind.
A woman at the long table says strangers walk up to look at the grain store and nobody here does.
A serjeant of the watch answers that strangers ask him where the grain is kept and never where the sick are.
A journeyman reckons what a stranger takes for plenty is a store the trades filled and cannot open.
The officers of the courts say a stranger's questions about the store are ordinary and his questions about the sick are new to them.

units.spine: The law is present here and so is the crime, and neither of the two has the run of the town. Nobody here calls the place safe, and nobody calls it dangerous.

units.poolKey: First-Survey qualification (the reading is a first look)
units.spine: The safety reading here rests on a first look. What that look took in stands in the reading, and what it missed stands nowhere.
A stranger here is not robbed but told quietly what the arrangement is, and what he is at risk of was arranged well before he arrived.
The hall at Rundgate moves against the criminal factions and the factions move back against the hall, and the town is where the two of them meet.
The town holds its own ways in. The walls and gates settle where anything arrives and nothing about what it brings.
The town keeps soldiers of its own. The garrison's work is the holding of this place, and the men who do it answer for it as work.
Some of the soldiers here are hired and the town knows which ones. The men out of the mercenary quarter are counted differently from the garrison, and counted openly.
A stranger finds halls here whose business is the kind of trouble a garrison is the wrong answer to. The adventurers' guilds are more than one, and none of them is short of work.
A stranger is measured at the gate in a way he cannot name, and nobody there tells him what was done.
The city walls and gates stand better than the watch that should be on them. The keeping of the stone is met and the wage on the wall comes short.

units.poolKey: Logistics & Supply: Granary with road supply
units.spine: The town keeps stores and is fed by the roads alone. What the grain store buys is the time to do something about a road.
